commitResults.messageTitle: Document the branch naming convention in AGENTS.md
commitResults.messageBody:
The Git conventions section of AGENTS.md covers commit message subjects
and bodies, but says nothing about branch names, although the se-edu
conventions it links to prescribe those too. Contributors have to follow
the link to find out how to name a branch, and it is easy to assume the
conventions govern issue titles and descriptions as well, which they do
not.

Let's record the branch naming rules alongside the commit message rules,
and state that the conventions stop at commit messages and branch names.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add Dillion's entry to the About Us page
commitResults.messageBody:
The About Us page lists the AB-3 sample team, so it names Jane Doe as
team lead and points at a placeholder photo. Readers of our project
website have no way to tell who is on the team.

Let's replace that placeholder with my own name, photo, profile links
and responsibilities.

commitResults.messageTitle: Revert "Add Dillion's entry to the About Us page"
commitResults.messageBody:
The About Us entries are meant to go out as parallel PRs from every
member at once, so that merging them gives us practice at resolving
conflicts. My entry lands ahead of that round. It also points at
docs/images/dillionlim.png, which sits in an unmerged PR, so the page
shows a broken image.

Let's take the entry back out and send it again together with the rest
of the team.

This reverts commit d99183a5517e7f56ff8bee89471910547607720b3.
Revert "Add Dillion's entry to the About Us page"

commitResults.messageTitle: Document the branch lifecycle rules in AGENTS.md
commitResults.messageBody:
The Git conventions section of AGENTS.md links only to the se-edu
conventions, which say nothing about what happens to a branch after its
PR merges. Admin Appendix E adds two rules of its own: branches must
survive the merge, and branches are synced by merging rather than
rebasing. Both exist because the course scripts read branches and commit
timestamps, so breaking either costs marks in a way that is invisible
from the diff.

Let's record both rules next to the branch naming convention, and note
that they come from the course admin pages rather than from se-edu.

commitResults.messageTitle: Rename AB3 packages and classes to TAB
commitResults.messageBody:
The codebase carries the names of the sample project it was forked
from: the root package is seedu.address, the model root is AddressBook,
and the entity every command operates on is Person. Our product is a
teaching assistant's student book, so every one of those names tells a
reader something untrue, and the mismatch grows more expensive the more
feature code we add on top of it.

Let's rename the root package to seedu.tab, AddressBook to StudentBook
and Person to Student, along with the files, packages, test fixtures and
data files named after them. Address stays, since it remains a field on
a student. The documentation is renamed separately.
Add Thang's photo
Edit Agents.md
Add Dillion's photo
Add Thang's entry to AboutUs page
Add See Jay's entry to the About Us page
Add Xinnan's entry to AboutUs page
Add Dillion's entry to the About Us page

commitResults.messageTitle: Close sub-issues when their parent is closed
commitResults.messageBody:
The issue tracker records each MVP feature as an epic with its user
stories linked beneath it. GitHub does not cascade a close down that
hierarchy, so closing an epic leaves every story under it open. The
tracker then shows work outstanding that is done, and the v1.2 burndown
reads wrong.

Let's add a workflow that closes the open sub-issues of any issue that
is closed, leaving a comment on each saying which parent closed it.
Close sub-issues when their parent is closed

commitResults.messageTitle: Update the target user profile and value prop
commitResults.messageBody:
The Developer Guide describes a user who has a need to manage a
significant number of contacts, and offers them contact management
faster than a mouse-driven GUI. That is AB3's audience and AB3's pitch,
so a reader of our own guide learns nothing about who TAB is for or why
they would pick it over a spreadsheet.

Let's replace both with the profile and value proposition the team
settled on: an NUS School of Computing teaching assistant running 2 to 3
tutorial or lab slots a semester, and a semester of students managed
faster than a spreadsheet or a mouse-driven contact app.

commitResults.messageTitle: Rewrite the user stories for TAB
commitResults.messageBody:
The Developer Guide lists six AB3 sample stories about hiding private
contact details and sorting persons, followed by a "more to be added"
placeholder. None of them describe what a teaching assistant needs, so
the section documents the requirements of the project we forked rather
than our own.

Let's replace them with the sixty stories the team gathered, each with a
priority, and record the stories we raised and decided against along
with the reason for dropping each.
Rewrite the user stories for TAB

commitResults.messageTitle: Add a use case for adding a student
commitResults.messageBody:
The Developer Guide carries AB3's sample use case for deleting a person,
followed by a "more to be added" placeholder. It names AddressBook as
the system and persons as the subject, so it documents neither what TAB
does nor the shape we intend our own use cases to take.

Let's replace it with the use case for adding a student, covering the
malformed detail, the possible duplicate, the unwritable data file and
the user abandoning partway, and name TAB as the system in the preamble.
Add a use case for adding a student

commitResults.messageTitle: Point AGENTS.md at the renamed packages
commitResults.messageBody:
AGENTS.md is the first file a contributor or an agent reads to orient
itself in this repository, and five of its pointers lead nowhere: the
main class, the source and test roots, the jar name and the test-utility
path all still name seedu.address, which the rename to seedu.tab
removed. It also calls docs/ a Jekyll site, which the move to MarkBind
ended.

Let's point all of them at what the repository holds.

commitResults.messageTitle: Accept names that real students have
commitResults.messageBody:
Name rejects anything outside letters, digits and spaces, so a teaching
assistant cannot record Ravi s/o Kumaran, Siti Nur-Aisyah, Sean O'Brien
or Ma Ying-jeou, nor any name written in a non-Latin script. Those names
are on the roster, and the slash is rejected only because the parser
happens to use it as a delimiter. The PE bug guidelines name this exact
case as a feature flaw.

Let's accept any name that carries an identity, requiring only that it
holds at least one letter or number and neither begins nor ends with
whitespace, judged against the whole of Unicode rather than ASCII. Four
fixtures encoded the old rule and no longer describe an invalid name, so
they move to a value that still is one.

commitResults.messageTitle: Store names in a normalized form
commitResults.messageBody:
A name is not only displayed. The search splits it into words on ASCII
whitespace, and isSameStudent compares it as the identity of a student.
The widened rule admits names that defeat both: John<NBSP>Doe cannot be
found by searching for John, and a leading zero-width space produces a
second student indistinguishable from the first. The review of #83
reproduced both, and the Developer Guide's claim that a name is never
parsed nor compared was wrong.

Let's normalize a name as it is constructed, composing it to NFC,
discarding the zero-width space and byte order mark, reducing runs of
any Unicode whitespace to one ASCII space and trimming the ends. The
joiner and non-joiner stay, because Sinhala and Arabic need them. The
rest of the application can then keep its ASCII assumption, and names
that look identical compare equal.

Surrounding whitespace is trimmed rather than rejected, which is what
the feature specification asks for. VALIDATION_REGEX described only half
the rule, so it gives way to two named patterns. AddCommandParserTest
covers the names end to end and pins the one the prefix syntax still
rejects, and both guides record the rule.

commitResults.messageTitle: Name: Widen the message and the whitespace tests
commitResults.messageBody:
Review of #83 raises two points. The constraint message says a name
needs a letter or a number, which reads oddly for a logographic script:
a reader with a Chinese name is told to supply a letter. The whitespace
tests cover only the space character, although the rule spans every kind
of Unicode whitespace.

Let's say letter, character or number, from any writing system, and
cover the tab, the line feed, the carriage return, the form feed, the
vertical tab, the em and thin spaces, the ogham space mark and the
ideographic space that a CJK input method produces.

commitResults.messageTitle: Name the fields an add command leaves out
commitResults.messageBody:
Leaving a field out of an add command prints the whole usage block,
including the example, and never says which field is missing. The user
has to compare their command against the example to find out. The PE bug
triaging guidelines call this out: an error message can be correct yet
give too many possible reasons without pointing at the specific one.

Only the first missing field would be worth naming if the parser stopped
at one, so it collects them all.

Let's have a prefix carry the name of the field it marks, and report the
fields that are missing rather than the format of the whole command.
Text before the first prefix is left alone: that is a malformed command
rather than an omitted field, and it keeps the usage block.

commitResults.messageTitle: MessagesTest: Cover the preconditions of both methods
commitResults.messageBody:
Codecov reports a partial branch on the assertion that guards
getErrorMessageForMissingPrefixes against being called with no prefixes.
The assertion is right, because a message that names no field at all
leaves the user with a colon and nothing after it, so the branch wants a
test rather than removal.

The method beside it carries the same assertion and has never had a test
of its own, and MessagesTest is a new file, so it may as well describe
the whole class.

Let's assert that each of the two rejects an empty call, and that the
older of them formats a single prefix as it always has.

commitResults.messageTitle: Read the field labels from the prefixes that own them
commitResults.messageBody:
Review of #85 raises three points.

The missing-field tests append a raw value where a prefix was dropped,
so the name under test also absorbs a stray number and each case fails
for two reasons at once. No case omits the name at all.

A field label such as NAME is now written twice, once where the prefix
is declared and again in the usage text of add and edit, so a rename
would leave the usage and the missing-field error disagreeing.

A test named for equals also asserts on hashCode.

Let's omit a field cleanly in each test and add the missing name, build
the usage text from the labels the prefixes carry, and give hashCode a
test of its own.

commitResults.messageTitle: Say what is wrong with a rejected value
commitResults.messageBody:
A value that fails validation is answered with the whole rule for its
field and no mention of what was typed. An email missing its @ earns
eight lines of specification, none of which say which character is
absent or quote the value. The PE bug triaging guidelines treat an
error message that gives too many possible reasons without pointing at
the specific one as a feature flaw.

Let's quote the value and give the reason. Each value class explains why
it turned a particular string down, and the parser composes that into
one line naming the field. Email distinguishes a missing at sign from a
doubled one, an empty local part, an empty domain, a malformed local
part and a final domain label shorter than two characters.

The full rule stays where someone looking for the format will read it,
and the data file keeps its own messages, since a reader repairing JSON
by hand wants the rule rather than a single value.
Name the fields an add command leaves out

commitResults.messageTitle: Accept the tags and phone numbers a roster holds
commitResults.messageBody:
A tag must match \p{Alnum}+, so Lab 3, Tutorial 5 and needs-followup are
all rejected, along with every tag in a non-Latin script. Those are the
tags the week 7 specification lists as valid parameters, and Lab 3 and
needs-followup are printed in docs/images/Ui.png. Week 5 records that
students are sliced by slot, module, semester, project team and status;
three of those five forms cannot be typed.

A phone number must match \d{3,}, so +65 9123 4567 is rejected, which is
how week 5 records that this user stores numbers. The PE bug triaging
guidelines use that case as their own example of overzealous validation.

Let's let both hold what a roster holds, asking only that a tag carries
a letter or a number and that a phone number carries three digits.
Neither is parsed, dialled or used to build a path, so no character in
either can hinder the app.

Name already stored a normalized form for the same reason, and a tag is
a key in a set, so the normalizer moves to StringUtil and all three
share it.

commitResults.messageTitle: Compose a field value after deleting from it
commitResults.messageBody:
Review of #86 finds three faults.

A zero-width character between a base letter and its combining mark
blocks the two from composing, and the normalizer composes before it
deletes. So "e" with a zero-width space and a combining acute is stored
as a decomposed pair, unequal to the single character it looks like, and
the search misses it. The fault reaches tags as well as names.

The reason given for a rejected name or tag says it holds no letter,
character or number, of a value such as --- that plainly holds
characters. A change made to give accurate reasons cannot itself
mislead.

The Developer Guide gives one rationale to three fields that do not
share it. Only a name is searched, and a phone number is neither an
identity nor a key in a set.

Let's delete first and compose last, say letter or number, and describe
each field by what is actually true of it. The method is renamed to
normalizeFieldValue, since it does more than whitespace, and a storage
test proves a phone number with a country code and a tag with a space
survive a save and a load.

commitResults.messageTitle: Name the field and the domain length once each
commitResults.messageBody:
Review of #86 asks about two literals.

ParserUtil writes the name of each field as a string where it composes
the message, so five names sit apart from the classes they describe and
nothing keeps them spelled the same way.

Email writes 2 twice, once in the regex for the last domain label and
once in the sentence that explains it, so the two can drift apart.

Let's give each value class the name it is reported under, and Email a
constant for the shortest last label it accepts.
Explain rejected values, and stop rejecting valid ones

commitResults.messageTitle: Report every fault in an add command at once
commitResults.messageBody:
The parser refuses a command at the first field it cannot accept, so a
user who mistyped the phone and the email is told about the phone,
corrects it, and only then learns about the email. Week 5 records the
complaint: supply a bad phone and a bad email and you round-trip twice.
A missing field and a bad value are reported separately for the same
reason, so leaving out the email while mistyping the phone also takes
two attempts.

Let's examine every field before refusing, and list what is wrong with
each on its own line. A field the command left out is reported once, as
missing, rather than again as a value that cannot be read.

ParseProblems holds the faults found so far and decides at the end
whether to stop, which keeps the parser reading as a list of fields
rather than as a chain of conditionals.

commitResults.messageTitle: Collect every bad tag, and bound the claim
commitResults.messageBody:
Review of #89 finds that the claim overreaches. A value before the first
prefix and a single-valued prefix given twice are both refused before
any field is read, and parseTags stops at the first tag it cannot
accept, so a command with two bad tags reports one.

The first two are not faults in a field. Until it is settled which value
belongs to which field, there is nothing to say about any of them, so
each is refused on its own. The third is the very fault this change
exists to remove and had simply been missed.

Let's parse each tag separately so that every bad one is reported, and
say in the guide and in the parser that fields are collected once the
shape of the command is settled, rather than claiming every mistake is
always gathered.

TAB-131 is marked cancelled in the story sheet and sits among the
stories the Developer Guide records as dropped, yet add still refuses a
command without an address. A teaching assistant therefore invents one
for every student, which is the thing TAB-125 exists to prevent for
email.

Let's take the field out of the student, the commands, the storage, the
card and the sample data.

Two consequences beyond the deletion. The a/ prefix goes with it, and
that prefix was what read a/l and a/p in a Malaysian name as the start
of another field, so those names now parse. And every data file written
so far holds an address key, which must keep loading; a fixture in that
older shape proves it does.

commitResults.messageTitle: StudentTest: Cover the hash of a student
commitResults.messageBody:
Codecov reports hashCode as uncovered. It is uncovered on master too,
and only reaches the patch because removing the address field changed
the line. Nothing has ever called it: a student is held in a list rather
than a hashed collection, so the method has no exercise.

Let's assert the contract, that two students which compare equal hash
alike, and that each remaining field reaches the hash.

commitResults.messageTitle: Take the address out of the guide and the diagrams
commitResults.messageBody:
Review of #91 finds the field still in three places.

The User Guide hands out four commands that hold an a/ fragment. With
the prefix gone the fragment joins the value before it, so the Betsy
example now fails on its email, and the example meant to show a phone
error never reaches the phone.

Both model diagrams still declare Address and draw the student pointing
at it, of a class the same change deletes.

The test for a file in the older shape checked three fields while the
description claimed the student loaded intact. Comparing the whole
student shows the claim was wrong for a different reason: the fixture
spelled the tag key tagged rather than tags, so the tag was dropped and
the narrower assertion passed anyway.

Let's correct the guide, the two diagrams and the fixture, compare the
whole student, and clear the comments and blank gaps the deletions left.

commitResults.messageTitle: Close the gaps a removed call left mid-chain
commitResults.messageBody:
Review of #91 finds two blank lines sitting inside a builder chain,
where the call that set the address used to be.

Let's close them.
Remove the cancelled address field

commitResults.messageTitle: Let a student be recorded without an email
commitResults.messageBody:
A teaching assistant meets a student, has a phone number and nothing
else, and cannot record them: add refuses the command without an
email, so an address gets invented to satisfy it. TAB-125 asks for the
opposite, that partial details be recorded as partial.

Let's hold the email as absent rather than as a made-up value. A
student keeps it as null and hands it out as an Optional, so a caller
has to decide what to do when there is none rather than meeting one by
accident. The card leaves its row out, the result box omits the field,
and a saved file simply carries no email key.

A file that holds an email keeps being checked: an address that is
present and malformed is still refused rather than quietly dropped.

commitResults.messageTitle: Record in both guides that the email is optional
commitResults.messageBody:
The User Guide gives add a format where the email is required, and the
Developer Guide describes three fields that must each hold something.
Neither now matches the command.

Let's mark the field optional in the format and the summary, say that
an email cannot be cleared once set, and record why the field is
nullable rather than an Optional.

commitResults.messageTitle: Test the student card on a headless toolkit
commitResults.messageBody:
The card decides whether to show an email and now has a branch that
nothing exercises. It cannot be tested as the project stands: building
one needs the JavaFX toolkit started, and a CI runner has no display,
so the class has never been covered at all.

Let's give the test task a headless toolkit through Monocle and cover
the card: an email that is present reaches the label, one that is absent
leaves the row out rather than leaving it blank, and the tags appear in
order.

StudentBuilder takes a null email, since a student without one is now
an ordinary student rather than an impossible one.

commitResults.messageTitle: Match the headless toolkit to the JavaFX version
commitResults.messageBody:
Platform.startup throws a NullPointerException on the runners. The
headless toolkit is version 21 while JavaFX here is 17, and the two
disagree about the native library the toolkit loads.

Let's take the toolkit at the version JavaFX is at, and drop the
properties that belong to a test robot this project does not use.

commitResults.messageTitle: Drop the headless toolkit from the test task
commitResults.messageBody:
The test task starts a Monocle toolkit so that the student card, and
the branch that decides whether to show an email, can be covered.
Monocle fails to start on every CI runner with a NullPointerException
out of Platform.startup, on both the 21.0.2 and the 17.0.10 release,
while the same run passes headless on a development machine. The build
therefore fails on ubuntu, macos and windows for a reason that has
nothing to do with the change under review.

Let's take the toolkit and the card test back out, so this branch is
judged on the optional email alone. A JavaFX test harness is worth
having, but it changes the build for every contributor and belongs in
a pull request the team weighs on its own merits.

commitResults.messageTitle: Give the storage test a real email to work with
commitResults.messageBody:
VALID_EMAIL in JsonAdaptedStudentTest reads BENSON.getEmail() and calls
toString on the result. That getter hands back an Optional, so the
constant holds the wrapper's text rather than johnd@example.com, and no
validator would accept it. Every test that passes the constant asserts
on a name, phone or tag fault that is raised before the email is looked
at, so they all pass without noticing.

Let's unwrap the Optional, and add a test that builds a student from
VALID_EMAIL and expects the address to survive, so a constant that
stops being an email is caught. The invalid-email test that repeats its
neighbour word for word goes with it.

commitResults.messageTitle: Leave build.gradle as this branch found it
commitResults.messageBody:
Taking the Monocle toolkit back out of the test task leaves behind the
blank line that its system properties sat under. That line is the only
mark the branch makes on build.gradle, so the file joins the diff
carrying nothing a reviewer can act on.

Let's remove it.

commitResults.messageTitle: Leave the email out of a saved file
commitResults.messageBody:
The Developer Guide says a saved file carries no email key for a student
who has none. Jackson writes every field it is handed, so the file holds
an email set to null instead. Anyone opening the file by hand meets a
schema the guide does not describe, and a null is an awkward thing to
ask a reader to edit around.

Let's have the adapted student drop a null field, and test that a
student without an email survives a save and a reload with no key
written. StudentBuilder gains a spelling for such a student, which the
tests here and the ones after it need.

commitResults.messageTitle: Stop presenting the email as required
commitResults.messageBody:
Three places still say that every student has an email. The add
command's usage text lists the email prefix unbracketed, so a user who
mistypes the command is told to supply one. The User Guide shows a
refusal naming the email among the missing fields, which the parser no
longer hands back. The Student class promises that its details are
present and not null, which its own constructor contradicts.

Let's bracket the prefix, replace the example with a refusal the parser
does produce, and have the class say what the constructor already does.

commitResults.messageTitle: Cover the student who has no email
commitResults.messageBody:
The suite holds no student without an email, so the state this change
exists to allow goes untested. Adding one, editing another of their
fields, giving them an email later, and comparing two of them all run
against fixtures that carry one, and a regression in the feature would
pass the suite.

Let's test each of those, so that an email that quietly reappears or
goes missing is caught.

commitResults.messageTitle: Give the Linux CI job a display
commitResults.messageBody:
The macOS and Windows runners carry a desktop session, so JavaFX starts
a toolkit there and a test may build a UI node. The Linux runner has
none, and GtkApplication refuses with "Unable to open DISPLAY", so a
test that touches the UI passes on two platforms out of three. The
Linux job is also the one that uploads coverage, so the UI classes can
never be reported as covered.

Let's run a virtual display on that job, so every platform can exercise
the UI classes.

The card decides whether to show an email, and nothing exercises either
branch. The class has no test at all, so the row that a student without
an email is meant to leave out is checked only by eye.

Let's cover the card: an email that is present reaches the label, one
that is absent leaves the row unmanaged rather than blank, a name and
phone carrying symbols arrive as given, and the tags are shown in
order.

commitResults.messageTitle: Load a hand-edited file that spells no email
commitResults.messageBody:
The tests reach an absent email by handing the adapted student a Java
null, which skips Jackson and the storage layer entirely. A file edited
by hand is where an absent email really arrives, and it may spell one
two ways: the key set to null, or the key left out. Neither is read by
any test, though this change alters what the file is allowed to hold.

Let's add a fixture holding both spellings and load it through storage,
so a student who has no email survives the trip from disk.

commitResults.messageTitle: Say that the email is optional where it is described
commitResults.messageBody:
The model diagrams draw an unqualified line from a student to an email,
which reads as one the student must have. The card explains that it
hides the row to avoid a gap "where the address used to be", naming a
field the project no longer holds. The add parser says that an absent
prefix is already reported as missing, which stopped being true when
the email became optional.

Let's mark the email end of the diagrams as 0..1 and correct both
comments.

commitResults.messageTitle: Pin the text of a result that has no email
commitResults.messageBody:
Messages.format leaves the email out for a student who has none. The
tests that exercise it build their expected result by calling format
itself, so they agree with whatever it produces and would not notice
"Email: null", a separator left behind, or another field dropped.

Let's assert the whole string for a student with an email, one without,
and one with neither an email nor a tag.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add a tokenizer for quoted command arguments
commitResults.messageBody:
The add command reads its fields from the n/ p/ e/ t/ prefixes, which a
value cannot itself hold: a name carrying p/ followed by a space is
read as the start of another field. The syntax that replaces them marks
fields with flags and takes the name as a positional value, and nothing
can be read from the arguments until they are split into tokens.

Let's add a tokenizer that splits on whitespace and lets double quotes
group a value holding spaces, or one opening with the hyphen that marks
a flag. A token remembers whether quotes took part in it, since that is
the only thing telling "-Ahmad" apart from an option. A quote left open
is reported as such, rather than surfacing later as a malformed field.

commitResults.messageTitle: Read a command as a name followed by flags
commitResults.messageBody:
A field marked by a prefix cannot appear inside a value, and a name is
exactly where such characters turn up: s/o survives only because no
field is marked s/, and a/l did not survive at all until the address
field was removed. Marking fields with flags and taking the name first
avoids the collision, but nothing can read that shape.

Let's add a reader for it over the tokenizer. The tokens before the
first flag are the name, each flag takes the token after it, and a flag
may repeat where the field allows it. An unknown flag, a flag left
without a value, and a token belonging to no flag are each reported for
what they are. No command uses it yet.

commitResults.messageTitle: Take the fields of add as options
commitResults.messageBody:
A prefix has to be a sequence that a value never contains, and no such
sequence exists for a name. s/o, d/o, a/l and a/p are ordinary parts of
Singaporean and Malaysian names, and a/l was unreadable for as long as
the address field was marked a/. Widening the prefixes moves the
collision rather than removing it.

Let's read add as a name followed by options, NAME -p PHONE [-e EMAIL]
[-t TAG]..., so that a value is a whole token and a name is read as a
name however it is spelled. A value that holds spaces, or opens with
the option marker, goes in double quotes.

edit keeps its prefixes for now. Its fields are all optional and it has
no positional value to protect, so it gains nothing from the change.

commitResults.messageTitle: Document how add reads its arguments
commitResults.messageBody:
The guides describe add as taking prefixes, down to the warning that a
name holding p/ is unreadable, which the new syntax removes. Nothing
records why the command reads differently from the rest either.

Let's rewrite the add section of the User Guide, say in the notes that
the two spellings exist side by side, and explain the two parsing
passes and the reason for them in the Developer Guide. A test reads the
worked examples back out of the User Guide and parses each one, since a
guide handing out a command the app refuses is a bug whichever of the
two is wrong.

commitResults.messageTitle: Test the flag type and the messages about flags
commitResults.messageBody:
Flag carries the equality that lets a map find the values given for a
field, and the two new message helpers each hold a precondition, yet
none of them is reached by a test. A lone hyphen decides whether a
token marks a field, and nothing gives it one either.

Let's test Flag the way Prefix is already tested, assert both new
messages including the precondition they carry, and give the tokenizer
a hyphen standing on its own.

commitResults.messageTitle: Keep the new parser classes from being instantiated
commitResults.messageBody:
CliFlags, CommandTokenizer and FlagTokenizer hold only static members,
so the compiler gives each a public constructor that means nothing. A
reader may reasonably build one and find it useless, and the coverage
report counts a constructor nobody calls against the change.

Let's make each constructor private. JaCoCo leaves out an empty private
constructor in a class of static members, so the three classes report
as fully covered, which they are.

The three parser classes that came before them still carry the implicit
constructor. Giving them the same treatment belongs in its own change.

commitResults.messageTitle: Read an option in the value position as a missing value
commitResults.messageBody:
An option takes whatever token follows it, without asking what that
token is. So `add John -p 123 -t -e` stores "-e" as a tag and reports
nothing, and `add John -p -e john@example.com` takes "-e" as the phone
and then complains about the address instead of the empty phone. Both
are plain mistakes, and both are read as something the user did not
write.

Let's treat an unquoted option where a value belongs as the option
before it having been left empty, and say which field needs the value.
A value that really does open with a hyphen is given in quotes, so the
message says so.

commitResults.messageTitle: Let a value hold a quote or a backslash
commitResults.messageBody:
A double quote is syntax with no way to escape it, so it is stripped
wherever it appears: `add Dwayne "The Rock" Johnson` stores the name
without its quotes and says nothing. Name accepts any punctuation as
long as a letter or number remains, and a tag may hold a quote too, so
the tokenizer silently discards characters the fields allow.

Let's read a backslash before a quote or another backslash as that
character. A backslash before anything else stays where it is, so a
value gains no new way to lose characters.

commitResults.messageTitle: Record that edit still collides with its prefixes
commitResults.messageBody:
The Developer Guide says edit gains nothing from options. It does: the
collision the options remove from add is still there, and `edit 1
n/John p/ Smith` reads Smith as a phone number, so a name add accepts
cannot be typed into edit at all. Two commands reading differently is a
second problem on top of that one. The usage text and the Prefix
javadoc also describe the syntax wrongly, and an undo diagram shows a
command that no longer parses.

Let's say what the limitation is in both guides, warn the reader of the
User Guide where edit is described, point at issue #105 for converting
it, and correct the three stale descriptions.
Add PR review guidelines to AGENTS.md

commitResults.messageTitle: Call the value before the options a preamble
commitResults.messageBody:
FlagArgumentMap and FlagTokenizer sit beside ArgumentMultimap as the
shared way to read a command, yet they call the value before the first
option a name. Only add reads it as a name. edit, which issue #105 is
about converting, would read an index there, and would have to ask for
getName to get one.

Let's call it the preamble, the word ArgumentMultimap already uses for
the same position, and leave the label NAME with the command that takes
a name.

commitResults.messageTitle: Tidy the parser internals a reviewer walked through
commitResults.messageBody:
A few things read worse than they work. Two flags sharing a marker
throw out of the collector rather than being read as one field. put
takes the defensive copy that getAllValues makes for its callers,
mutates it, and puts it back. The duplicate-field message collects into
a set, so the fields can be named in a different order from one run to
the next. One assertion compares a boolean against true.

Let's merge duplicate markers, build the list in place, keep the order
the fields were given in, and assert the boolean directly.

commitResults.messageTitle: Answer a stray value without guessing why it is there
commitResults.messageBody:
The message for a value belonging to no option says a name holding
spaces needs quotes. That is one cause out of several and wrong about
the rest: a quoted name given after the options is already quoted, a
second tag written without repeating the option is not a name, and a
value left over from a typing slip is neither. The tokenizer still
documents that a quote cannot appear in a value, which stopped being
true when the escape was added, and the tip that teaches quoting uses a
name holding a slash, which needs no quotes at all.

Let's state the three rules a stray value can break rather than naming
one cause, and correct every description of the quoting rule that says
more than it should.

commitResults.messageTitle: Say preamble in the summary as well as the body
commitResults.messageBody:
FlagTokenizer's class javadoc opens by saying it reads a name followed
by flagged fields, while the paragraph under it says preamble. The
rename reached the paragraph and not the sentence above it, so the
class contradicts itself on the first line a reader meets. The same
sentence about a value opening with the flag marker calls it a name.

Let's finish the rename in both places.

commitResults.messageTitle: Split a command on a pasted non-breaking space
commitResults.messageBody:
The tokenizer splits on Character.isWhitespace, which leaves out the
non-breaking space. A field value is normalized with a pattern that
does match it, so the two disagree about what separates one value from
the next, and the disagreement is invisible until it bites.

A command pasted from a web page or a chat message carries non-breaking
spaces. One between a name and an option reports the phone as missing
while "-p 91234567" sits plainly in the command, and one after an
option reports that there is no "-p 91234567" option. Both read as the
app failing to see what the user typed.

Let's put the decision in StringUtil beside the pattern that normalizes
a field, and have the tokenizer ask it, so the two cannot drift apart
again. The ideographic space a Chinese keyboard produces is covered by
the same change.

commitResults.messageTitle: Take the whitespace rule from the pattern itself
commitResults.messageBody:
isWhitespace names the characters that separate one value from the
next, and its javadoc claims that this keeps it agreeing with the
pattern normalizeFieldValue collapses with. It does not. U+0085 is
matched by the pattern and by neither Character method, and U+001C is
claimed by Character and not by the pattern, so the two disagree in
both directions. Naming the characters was the same mistake as having
two definitions, only harder to see.

Let's ask the pattern rather than restate it, and check every value a
char can hold against it, so the agreement is a fact rather than a
claim. The cost is a small string per character of a typed command,
which no user will notice.

commitResults.messageTitle: Ask the one whitespace pattern there is
commitResults.messageBody:
isWhitespace matches against a second pattern spelling the same rule as
the one normalizeFieldValue collapses with. Two patterns that have to
stay identical are the drift the method was written to remove, moved
one line further down.

Let's use the pattern already there. Matching one or more whitespace
characters against a single character is the same as matching one, and
the agreement is then with the pattern itself rather than with a copy
of it.

UC01, UC02, and UC04 split a single command entry across separate user actions. This does not reflect how the CLI receives command words and arguments.

UC01 repeats the same duplicate warning in two extensions, which hides the decision that separates their outcomes.

commitResults.messageBody:
The use case table of contents stops at UC09 even though UC10 appears in the same section. Readers cannot navigate to the final use case from the index.

UC01's command-correction extension already resubmits the complete command. Resuming at step 1 would ask the User to enter it twice.

Let's continue at the save step after the corrected submission.

Direct outcomes in three affected extensions use nested-list indentation even though they have no nested step. MarkBind renders those outcomes as code blocks.

Let's align them with their top-level extension items so they render as prose.

The use case index uses GitHub-style slugs, but MarkBind generates different heading IDs for punctuation. All ten links therefore miss their sections.

Let's point each entry at the anchor generated by the project documentation build.

The follow-up option uses only the terse -f marker, which makes the
command less self-explanatory while reading or writing it.

Let's make --follow-up the primary marker and retain -f as an alias for
concise input and compatibility.
